# Engage: How Has the Amount of Sunlight Reaching Earth Varied in the Past? {#esd-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🧊 The Investigative Phenomenon

**The amount of radiation (sunlight) received at 65° N has gone up and down over the last 750,000 years, and it repeats a pattern about every 100,000 years.**

- Scientists get Earth's past temperatures from **ice cores, tree rings, and ocean sediments**. Ice cores reach back about **800,000 years**.
- They use the same kinds of data plus **mathematical models** of Earth's orbit to work out how much sunlight reached Earth over that time.
- Over the last 400,000 years, ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere have **grown and shrunk again and again**.

**Questions for this chapter:** How do we know natural cycles aren't causing climate change today? How has Earth's position relative to the Sun changed? Does the Sun's own output change?
:::

### Why 65° N in summer?

- **Ice sheets** (the key to ice ages) grow on land at **high northern latitudes**: Canada, Scandinavia, Siberia, Alaska and Greenland all sit near **65° N**.
- Snow falls there every winter. What matters is whether **summer sunlight** is strong enough to **melt it**. Weak summers → snow survives → ice sheets grow.
- Scientists have found a strong **correlation** between **summer sunlight at 65° N** and **glacial-interglacial cycles**.

```{ojs}
{

}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdBuildQuiz = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="margin:18px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button style="
      display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;
      background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0b7285 0%,#0a3d62 100%);
      color:#fff;border:none;padding:9px 22px;border-radius:50px;min-height:44px;
      font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;
      box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(11,114,133,.45);">
      <span style="font-size:1.1em;">📝</span> ${title}
      <span class="chevron" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="
      max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;
      transition:max-height .5s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1),opacity .4s ease,margin-top .3s ease;
      margin-top:0;text-align:left;">
      <button class="close-btn" style="
        display:block;margin:0 auto 10px auto;
        background:rgba(11,114,133,.15);color:#0b7285;border:none;
        padding:5px 18px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.85em;min-height:36px;
        font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;">Hide Quiz</button>
      <p style="text-align:center;opacity:.8;font-style:italic;font-size:.9em;margin-bottom:12px;">
        Select an answer for each question.</p>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  const closeBtn = body.querySelector(".close-btn");
  function expand(){ body.style.maxHeight="4000px";body.style.opacity="1";body.style.marginTop="14px";chevron.style.transform="rotate(180deg)"; }
  function collapse(){ body.style.maxHeight="0";body.style.opacity="0";body.style.marginTop="0";chevron.style.transform="rotate(0)"; }
  toggle.onclick = () => body.style.maxHeight === "0px" || body.style.maxHeight === "" ? expand() : collapse();
  closeBtn.onclick = collapse;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.className = "esd-opt";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        const all = card.querySelectorAll("button.esd-opt");
        all.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";
          all[qq.correct].style.borderColor="#48bb78";
          all[qq.correct].style.background="#f0fff4";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    fb.className = "esd-fb";
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  return outer;
}
```

## Radiation and Temperature During Earth's Past {#esd-radiation-temperature}

Your packet's graph shows **July sunlight at 65° N** (top) and **Antarctic temperature compared to today** (bottom). The interactive below uses the **real data** behind graphs like it. Hover or tap to read values. Yellow bands = **interglacials** (IG, warm periods like today). The cold stretches between them are **glacials** (ice ages).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof esdSpan = Inputs.radio(["Last 350,000 years (like your packet)", "Last 800,000 years"], {value: "Last 350,000 years (like your packet)", label: "Show:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdIG = {
  const out = [];
  let run = null;
  for (const d of esdEdc) {
    if (d.T > -1) {
      if (run && d.t - run[1] <= 2) run[1] = d.t;
      else { if (run) out.push(run); run = [d.t, d.t]; }
    }
  }
  if (run) out.push(run);
  return out.filter(r => r[1] - r[0] >= 3).map(r => ({x1: r[0], x2: r[1] + 1, mid: (r[0] + r[1] + 1) / 2}));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdHistoryChart = function(maxT, marks = []) {
  const orb = esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= maxT);
  const tem = esdEdc.filter(d => d.t <= maxT);
  const ig = esdIG.filter(b => b.x1 <= maxT);
  const W = Math.max(300, width);
  const xs = {domain: [maxT, 0], label: "Thousands of years ago", tickFormat: d => d};
  const top = Plot.plot({
    width: W, height: 220, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 30,
    x: {...xs, label: null},
    y: {label: "July sunlight at 65° N (W/m²)", domain: [380, 510], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect(ig, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 380, y2: 510, fill: "#facc15", fillOpacity: 0.28}),
      Plot.line(orb, {x: "t", y: "jul", stroke: "#d97706", strokeWidth: 2}),
      ...marks.filter(m => m.t <= maxT).map(m => Plot.text([m], {x: "t", y: d => esdOrbit[d.t].jul, text: () => "✕", fill: m.color, fontSize: 18, fontWeight: "bold"})),
      ...marks.filter(m => m.t <= maxT).map(m => Plot.text([m], {x: "t", y: d => esdOrbit[d.t].jul, text: () => m.label, fill: m.color, dy: -14, fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold"})),
      Plot.tip(orb, Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "jul", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\nJuly sunlight at 65° N: ${d.jul} W/m²`}))
    ]
  });
  const bottom = Plot.plot({
    width: W, height: 220, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
    x: xs,
    y: {label: "Temperature vs. today (°C)", domain: [-11, 5], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect(ig, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -11, y2: 5, fill: "#facc15", fillOpacity: 0.28}),
      Plot.text(ig, {x: "mid", y: 4.2, text: () => "IG", fill: "#b91c1c", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: 11}),
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.line(tem, {x: "t", y: "T", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
      ...marks.filter(m => m.t <= maxT).map(m => Plot.dot([m], {x: "t", y: d => esdEdcAt(d.t), r: 6, stroke: m.color, strokeWidth: 2.5})),
      Plot.tip(tem, Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "T", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\nTemperature: ${d.T > 0 ? "+" : ""}${d.T} °C vs. today`}))
    ]
  });
  return html`<div>${top}${bottom}<p class="esd-caption">Sunlight: mid-July daily average at the top of the atmosphere at 65° N, calculated from Earth's orbit (Berger &amp; Loutre 1991, NOAA). Temperature: EPICA Dome C ice core, East Antarctica (Jouzel et al. 2007, NOAA), compared to the last 1,000 years. Your packet's graph uses the nearby Dome Fuji core, which shows the same pattern.</p></div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdEdcAt = t => { const d = esdEdc.find(e => e.t === t); return d ? d.T : null; }
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdBuildQuiz("esd-engage-quiz", "🧊 Check Your Understanding: Reading the Graph", [
  {
    q: "Count the yellow interglacial bands in the last 350,000 years. About how often does Earth return to a warm interglacial?",
    options: ["About every 1,000 years", "About every 10,000 years", "About every 100,000 years", "Only once"],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Interglacials peak near 10, 125, 240 and 330 thousand years ago, roughly 100,000 years apart. Each one is short (about 10,000 to 15,000 years) compared with the long, cold glacial between them."
  },
  {
    q: "Look at the orange July sunlight curve. Which description fits best?",
    options: ["It stays almost flat", "It rises and falls in many smaller wiggles about every 20,000 years, and the size of the wiggles changes", "It only goes up", "It has exactly one peak every 100,000 years"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "July sunlight at 65° N swings between roughly 390 and 500 W/m² in waves about 19,000 to 23,000 years apart. The waves get bigger and smaller over about 100,000 years. Each time an interglacial starts, a big sunlight peak is happening."
  },
  {
    q: "Warm interglacials line up with high summer sunlight. What can we say so far?",
    options: ["We have proven that sunlight causes interglacials", "The two are correlated (they rise and fall together), but we need more evidence about the mechanism to claim cause and effect", "There is no relationship", "Temperature controls the Sun"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "A correlation means two things change together. To claim causation we need evidence of HOW one causes the other, which is what the models in this chapter are for. Notice too that some big sunlight peaks (like 218 thousand years ago) did not start an interglacial."
  }
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Radiation and Temperature During Earth's Past

Use the graph to fill in the **See-Think-Wonder** table:

| See: What did you observe? | Think: What do these observations make you think? | Wonder |
|---|---|---|
| What pattern do you observe in the **frequency of interglacial and glacial periods**? | What do you think might be **causing** these interglacial and glacial periods? | What questions do you have? |
| What pattern do you observe in the **July insolation** graph? | What **factors** do you think influence the amount of insolation reaching Earth at 65° N in July? | |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

Ideas scientists (and classes) come up with:

- **See:** The total insolation at 65° N **rises and falls** over time on a scale of **thousands of years**. Glacial and interglacial periods also change in a pattern: a warm interglacial about every **100,000 years**, with some exceptions.
- **See:** There are smaller insolation peaks between the big ones. The pattern repeats, but there are also **irregularities**.
- **Think:** When insolation is highest, Earth tends to be in an **interglacial**, so there seems to be a **relationship** between insolation and glacial periods.
- **Think:** **Earth's position relative to the Sun** could change how much sunlight reaches 65° N. The **amount of energy the Sun gives off** might change it too.
- **Wonder:** *How does the amount of insolation change? How does it affect glacial and interglacial periods? Why aren't the two graphs perfectly lined up?*
:::

::: {.key-idea}
**🔑 Correlation vs. causation**

- **Correlation:** two things rise and fall together.
- **Causation:** one thing actually **makes** the other happen.
- To claim causation you need **empirical evidence of a mechanism**, and you need to rule out other possible causes. In this chapter you'll test two possible causes: **Earth's orbit** and **the Sun's output**.
:::

# Explore: How Does Earth's Position Affect the Amount of Radiation Reaching Earth's Surface? {#esd-explore}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔬 Three Ways Earth's Position Changes

As Earth orbits the Sun, three things slowly change over **tens and hundreds of thousands of years**:

1. **The direction of Earth's tilt** with respect to the Sun (*precession*)
2. **The degree of Earth's tilt** (*obliquity*)
3. **The shape of Earth's orbit** (*eccentricity*)

Your job: describe how each one changes, then use a **model** to collect evidence. Can Earth's changing position explain the pattern of sunlight at 65° N?
:::

## Orbital Factors Investigation {#esd-orbital-factors-investigation}

### 🕰️ Orbit time machine

Drag the slider back in time. Watch the orbit's **shape**, the **tilt**, and **where Earth is during Northern Hemisphere (NH) summer** change. Use this to "draw a representation of how each factor changes over time."

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof esdT = Inputs.range([0, 800], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "Thousands of years ago:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof esdExag = Inputs.toggle({label: "Exaggerate shape ×8:", value: true})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const d = esdOrbit[esdT];
  const AU = 149.6;
  // ---- orbit, top view ----
  const W = 320, H = 240, sx = 165, sy = 120, a = 110;
  const eDraw = Math.min(esdExag ? d.e * 8 : d.e, 0.6);
  const c = a * eDraw, b = a * Math.sqrt(1 - eDraw * eDraw);
  const nuJ = ((270 - d.w) % 360 + 360) % 360;             // June solstice, degrees after perihelion
  const pos = nu => { const r = a * (1 - eDraw * eDraw) / (1 + eDraw * Math.cos(nu * Math.PI / 180)); const th = (180 + nu) * Math.PI / 180; return [sx + r * Math.cos(th), sy - r * Math.sin(th)]; };
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", `Top view of Earth's orbit ${esdT} thousand years ago`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("display", "block");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1d33");
  svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", sx + c).attr("cy", sy).attr("rx", a).attr("ry", b).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7dd3fc").attr("stroke-width", 1.5).attr("stroke-dasharray", "4,3");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", sx).attr("cy", sy).attr("r", 15).attr("fill", "#fbbf24");
  const peri = [sx + c - a, sy], aph = [sx + c + a, sy];
  svg.append("text").attr("x", peri[0] + 4).attr("y", sy + 22).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 10).text("closest");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", aph[0] - 4).attr("y", sy + 22).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 10).text("farthest");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", peri[0]).attr("cy", sy).attr("r", 2.5).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", aph[0]).attr("cy", sy).attr("r", 2.5).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0");
  const [jx, jy] = pos(nuJ), [dx, dy] = pos(nuJ + 180);
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", jx).attr("cy", jy).attr("r", 9).attr("fill", "#38bdf8").attr("stroke", "#fde68a").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", jx).attr("y", jy - 14).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", "bold").text("NH summer");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", dx).attr("cy", dy).attr("r", 7).attr("fill", "#38bdf8").attr("opacity", 0.6);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", dx).attr("y", dy - 12).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#bae6fd").attr("font-size", 10).text("NH winter");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 20).attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 13).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(esdT === 0 ? "Today" : `${esdT},000 years ago`);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", H - 10).attr("fill", "#94a3b8").attr("font-size", 9).text(esdExag ? "Shape exaggerated ×8 (real orbit looks almost circular)" : "True shape: almost a circle!");
  // ---- tilt, side view ----
  const W2 = 220, H2 = 240, ex = 125, ey = 125, R = 55, t = d.obl * Math.PI / 180;
  const s2 = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W2} ${H2}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", `Earth tilted ${d.obl.toFixed(2)} degrees`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("display", "block");
  s2.append("rect").attr("width", W2).attr("height", H2).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1d33");
  s2.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 20).attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 11).text("☀️ Sun this way (NH summer)");
  s2.append("circle").attr("cx", ex).attr("cy", ey).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#2563eb");
  s2.append("path").attr("d", `M${ex},${ey - R} A${R},${R} 0 0 1 ${ex},${ey + R} Z`).attr("fill", "rgba(0,0,0,.45)");
  s2.append("line").attr("x1", ex).attr("y1", ey - R * 1.45).attr("x2", ex).attr("y2", ey + R * 1.45).attr("stroke", "#94a3b8").attr("stroke-dasharray", "3,3");
  const nx = ex - Math.sin(t) * R * 1.45, ny = ey - Math.cos(t) * R * 1.45;
  s2.append("line").attr("x1", 2 * ex - nx).attr("y1", 2 * ey - ny).attr("x2", nx).attr("y2", ny).attr("stroke", "white").attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
  s2.append("text").attr("x", nx - 4).attr("y", ny - 4).attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 12).attr("font-weight", "bold").attr("text-anchor", "end").text("N");
  const arc = d3.arc()({innerRadius: R * 1.2, outerRadius: R * 1.22, startAngle: -t, endAngle: 0});
  s2.append("path").attr("d", arc).attr("transform", `translate(${ex},${ey})`).attr("fill", "#fde68a");
  s2.append("text").attr("x", ex + 6).attr("y", ey - R * 1.3).attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 12).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(`${d.obl.toFixed(2)}°`);
  const closer = Math.cos(nuJ * Math.PI / 180) > 0;
  const rJ = AU * (1 - d.e * d.e) / (1 + d.e * Math.cos(nuJ * Math.PI / 180));
  return html`<div class="esd-row"><div>${svg.node()}</div><div style="max-width:260px;">${s2.node()}</div></div>
  <div class="esd-readout" style="max-width:640px;margin:8px auto;">
  <table class="esd-table">
  <tr><th>Factor</th><th>${esdT === 0 ? "Today" : esdT + ",000 years ago"}</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Shape of orbit (eccentricity)</td><td><b>${d.e.toFixed(4)}</b> → closest ${(AU * (1 - d.e)).toFixed(1)}, farthest ${(AU * (1 + d.e)).toFixed(1)} million km</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Degree of tilt (obliquity)</td><td><b>${d.obl.toFixed(2)}°</b></td></tr>
  <tr><td>Direction of tilt (precession)</td><td>NH summer happens when Earth is <b>${closer ? "closer to" : "farther from"}</b> the Sun (${rJ.toFixed(1)} million km)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>☀️ July sunlight at 65° N</td><td><b>${d.jul} W/m²</b> (today: 426.8)</td></tr>
  </table></div>`;
}
```

<p class="esd-caption">Orbital values: Berger &amp; Loutre (1991), NOAA Paleoclimatology. Distances use an average Earth-Sun distance of 149.6 million km.</p>

### 🔦 Virtual flashlight model

In class you shine a **flashlight on a sphere**. Here's the online version. The beam is the same width every time. Watch two things:

- **Total radiation reaching Earth** (does the whole planet get more or less?)
- **Radiation at 65° N** (does the beam get **spread out** over more ground?)

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof esdLab = Inputs.radio(["Direction of tilt", "Degree of tilt", "Distance from the Sun"], {value: "Direction of tilt", label: "Model:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdQ = (r, decl, lat = 65) => {
  const p = lat * Math.PI / 180, dd = decl * Math.PI / 180;
  const x = -Math.tan(p) * Math.tan(dd);
  const h = x <= -1 ? Math.PI : x >= 1 ? 0 : Math.acos(x);
  return 1361 / Math.PI * (149.6 / r) ** 2 * (h * Math.sin(p) * Math.sin(dd) + Math.cos(p) * Math.cos(dd) * Math.sin(h));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdFlashPanel = function(cfg) {
  const W = 300, H = 230, cx = 205, cy = 120, R = 72, dd = cfg.decl * Math.PI / 180, lat = 65 * Math.PI / 180;
  const alt = 90 - 65 + cfg.decl;
  const S = 1361 * (149.6 / cfg.r) ** 2;
  const Q = esdQ(cfg.r, cfg.decl);
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", `Flashlight model: ${cfg.title}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("display", "block");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1d33");
  // 65N point on the sunward limb
  const al = Math.PI + dd - lat;
  const py = cy - R * Math.sin(al);
  const bright = Math.max(0.15, Math.min(1, 0.55 + (S - 1361) / 120));
  const rays = d3.range(-7, 7.01, 2.33).map(o => py + o);
  const hits = [];
  rays.forEach(y => {
    const dy = y - cy;
    const hx = Math.abs(dy) < R ? cx - Math.sqrt(R * R - dy * dy) : W;
    if (Math.abs(dy) < R) hits.push([hx, y]);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", 28).attr("y1", y).attr("x2", hx).attr("y2", y).attr("stroke", "#fde047").attr("stroke-opacity", bright).attr("stroke-width", 1.6);
  });
  svg.append("rect").attr("x", 6).attr("y", py - 11).attr("width", 24).attr("height", 22).attr("rx", 4).attr("fill", "#94a3b8");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 18).attr("y", py + 26).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 9).text("flashlight");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#2563eb");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", `M${cx},${cy - R} A${R},${R} 0 0 1 ${cx},${cy + R} Z`).attr("fill", "rgba(0,0,0,.45)");
  const P = [-Math.sin(dd), -Math.cos(dd)], Qv = [Math.cos(dd), -Math.sin(dd)];
  const chord = (phi, col, w) => {
    const m = [cx + R * Math.sin(phi) * P[0], cy + R * Math.sin(phi) * P[1]], h = R * Math.cos(phi);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", m[0] - h * Qv[0]).attr("y1", m[1] - h * Qv[1]).attr("x2", m[0] + h * Qv[0]).attr("y2", m[1] + h * Qv[1]).attr("stroke", col).attr("stroke-width", w);
  };
  chord(0, "#cbd5e1", 1);
  chord(lat, "#fb923c", 2);
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx - P[0] * R * 1.3).attr("y1", cy - P[1] * R * 1.3).attr("x2", cx + P[0] * R * 1.3).attr("y2", cy + P[1] * R * 1.3).attr("stroke", "white").attr("stroke-width", 2);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + P[0] * R * 1.38).attr("y", cy + P[1] * R * 1.38).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", "bold").text("N");
  if (hits.length > 1) {
    const a0 = Math.atan2(-(hits[0][1] - cy), hits[0][0] - cx), a1 = Math.atan2(-(hits[hits.length - 1][1] - cy), hits[hits.length - 1][0] - cx);
    const pts = d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.05).map(f => { const aa = a0 + (a1 - a0) * f; return [cx + R * Math.cos(aa), cy - R * Math.sin(aa)]; });
    svg.append("path").attr("d", d3.line()(pts)).attr("stroke", "#fde047").attr("stroke-width", 6).attr("stroke-opacity", Math.max(0.25, bright * Math.sin(alt * Math.PI / 180) + 0.15)).attr("fill", "none");
  }
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + R * Math.cos(al) - 6).attr("y", py - 12).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("fill", "#fb923c").attr("font-size", 10).attr("font-weight", "bold").text("65° N");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 18).attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 12).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(cfg.title);
  const spread = alt > 0.5 ? 1 / Math.sin(alt * Math.PI / 180) : Infinity;
  return html`<div>${svg.node()}<div class="esd-readout">
    🌍 Total radiation reaching Earth: <b>${S.toFixed(0)} W/m²</b><br>
    📐 Noon Sun angle at 65° N: <b>${alt.toFixed(1)}°</b> above the horizon<br>
    🔦 Beam spread at 65° N: <b>${spread === Infinity ? "misses" : spread.toFixed(1) + "×"}</b> the beam's width<br>
    ☀️ Daily average sunlight at 65° N: <b>${Q.toFixed(0)} W/m²</b></div></div>`;
}
```

### Factor 1: The direction of Earth's tilt {#esd-direction-of-tilt}

- Earth's axis **wobbles like a spinning top**, tracing a circle about every **26,000 years** (*axial precession*).
- Meanwhile the orbit itself slowly turns. Together they move the seasons around the orbit, so **NH summer lines up with Earth's closest point about every 23,000 years** (cycles range from about **19,000 to 24,000 years**).
- **Two extremes:** NH tilted **toward** the Sun when Earth is closest (stronger NH summers) vs. NH tilted **away** from the Sun when closest (weaker NH summers, like **today**: Earth is closest on about **January 3**).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Direction of tilt over the last 200,000 years",
  subtitle: "Up = NH summer happens closer to the Sun. Count the peaks!",
  width: Math.max(300, width), height: 220, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {domain: [200, 0], label: "Thousands of years ago"},
  y: {label: "Precession index", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.line(esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= 200), {x: "t", y: "closeness", stroke: "#7c3aed", strokeWidth: 2}),
    ...(esdT <= 200 ? [Plot.ruleX([esdT], {stroke: "#e8590c", strokeWidth: 2})] : []),
    Plot.tip(esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= 200), Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "closeness", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\n${d.closeness > 0 ? "NH summer closer to Sun" : "NH summer farther from Sun"}`}))
  ]
})
```

<p class="esd-caption">Precession index = −e·sin(ϖ) from Berger &amp; Loutre (1991). The orange line is the time-machine slider.</p>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdBuildQuiz("esd-direction-quiz", "🔄 Check: Direction of Tilt", [
  {
    q: "In the flashlight model, the NH is tilted toward the Sun and then away. Does the TOTAL radiation reaching Earth change?",
    options: ["Yes, it doubles", "No. Earth is the same distance from the Sun, so the whole planet gets the same total (1,361 W/m²)", "Yes, it drops to zero", "Only at night"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Tilting doesn't move Earth closer or farther, so the total sunlight hitting the planet stays the same. The tilt only changes WHERE the sunlight lands."
  },
  {
    q: "What happens to radiation at 65° N when the NH is tilted away from the Sun?",
    options: ["It increases", "The Sun is only about 1.6° above the horizon at noon, so the beam is spread very thin and 65° N gets almost no sunlight", "It stays the same", "It moves to the equator only"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Tilted away, 65° N is near the edge of the lit side. The beam hits at a very low angle and spreads over a huge area. The daily average drops from about 494 to about 3 W/m²: that's winter."
  }
])
```

### Factor 2: The degree of Earth's tilt {#esd-degree-of-tilt}

- Earth's tilt (*obliquity*) slowly rocks between about **22.1° and 24.5°** and back, about every **41,000 years**.
- Today it is **23.44°** and **decreasing**. It was last at its maximum about **10,000 years ago** and will reach its minimum in about 10,000 years.
- **More tilt** → summer Sun climbs higher at high latitudes → **stronger summers** (and colder winters).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Degree of tilt over the last 400,000 years",
  subtitle: "Count the peaks to find the cycle length",
  width: Math.max(300, width), height: 220, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {domain: [400, 0], label: "Thousands of years ago"},
  y: {label: "Tilt (degrees)", domain: [22, 24.6], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= 400), {x: "t", y: "obl", stroke: "#0b7285", strokeWidth: 2}),
    ...(esdT <= 400 ? [Plot.ruleX([esdT], {stroke: "#e8590c", strokeWidth: 2})] : []),
    Plot.tip(esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= 400), Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "obl", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\nTilt: ${d.obl}°`}))
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}

    options: ["The noon Sun is higher (47.1° → 49.5°), so the beam is less spread out and summer sunlight rises from about 472 to 512 W/m²", "Nothing changes", "Sunlight at 65° N decreases", "Total radiation reaching Earth doubles"],

    explanation: "More tilt aims high northern latitudes more directly at the Sun in summer. The total reaching the whole planet stays the same (same distance); it's the distribution that changes."
  }
])
```

- **Model** it: observations when Earth is **less tilted** vs. **more tilted** toward the Sun.
- **Q1:** Does the **total** radiation reaching Earth change? **Q2:** Does the radiation **at 65° N** change? Give evidence for both.
:::

### Factor 3: The shape of Earth's orbit (eccentricity) {#esd-eccentricity}

- Earth's orbit stretches from **nearly circular (eccentricity ≈ 0.0034)** to **slightly oval (≈ 0.058)** and back.
- Main cycles: about **100,000 years**, plus a longer **405,000-year** cycle.
- Today it is **0.0167**: Earth is about **147.1 million km** from the Sun in early January and **152.1 million km** in early July. That's only a **~3%** difference in distance (about **7%** in sunlight).
- A more oval orbit makes the **difference between closest and farthest bigger**, so it makes the direction-of-tilt effect **stronger**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Shape of Earth's orbit over the last 800,000 years",
  subtitle: "0 = perfect circle. Find the ~100,000-year and ~405,000-year cycles.",
  width: Math.max(300, width), height: 220, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {domain: [800, 0], label: "Thousands of years ago"},
  y: {label: "Eccentricity", domain: [0, 0.06], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(esdOrbit, {x: "t", y: "e", fill: "#38bdf8", fillOpacity: 0.25}),
    Plot.line(esdOrbit, {x: "t", y: "e", stroke: "#0284c7", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([esdT], {stroke: "#e8590c", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.tip(esdOrbit, Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "e", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\nEccentricity: ${d.e}\nClosest ${(149.6 * (1 - d.e)).toFixed(1)} / farthest ${(149.6 * (1 + d.e)).toFixed(1)} million km`}))
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdBuildQuiz("esd-ecc-quiz", "🥚 Check: Shape of the Orbit", [
  {
    q: "In the distance model, Earth moves from 147.1 to 152.1 million km. What changes?",
    options: ["Only the radiation at 65° N", "The TOTAL radiation reaching Earth drops (about 1,408 → 1,317 W/m², about 7%), and 65° N gets less too", "Nothing; distance doesn't matter", "The tilt changes"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Light spreads out as it travels, so a farther Earth gets less everywhere. This is the only one of the three factors that changes the total amount of radiation reaching Earth."
  },
  {
    q: "Today Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why isn't January summer in New York?",
    options: ["Because the NH is tilted away from the Sun in January, and tilt matters more than the small change in distance", "Because the Sun is dimmer in January", "Because Earth is actually farthest in January", "Because of clouds"],
    correct: 0,
    explanation: "The distance changes only about 3%, but tilt changes the Sun's angle a lot. In January the NH is tilted away, so NH winter happens even though Earth is closest."
  }
])
```

### ✏️ In your packet: The shape of Earth's orbit (eccentricity)

- **Draw** how this factor changes over time. **How long is a full cycle?**
- **Model** it: observations at a **shorter** vs. **longer** distance between Earth and the Sun.
- **Q1:** Does the **total** radiation reaching Earth change? **Q2:** Does the radiation **at 65° N** change? Give evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Orbital Factors answers (try it first!)

| Factor | Full cycle | Total radiation reaching Earth changes? | Radiation at 65° N changes? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direction of tilt** (precession) | ~26,000 years for the wobble; NH summer lines up with closest approach about every ~23,000 years | **No.** Same distance, same total | **Yes.** Tilted toward → high noon Sun, concentrated beam. Tilted away → very low Sun, beam spread out |
| **Degree of tilt** (obliquity) | ~41,000 years (22.1° ↔ 24.5°) | **No.** Same distance, same total | **Yes.** More tilt → higher summer Sun at 65° N → more concentrated summer sunlight |
| **Shape of orbit** (eccentricity) | ~100,000 years (also ~405,000) | **Yes.** Closer → more total radiation; farther → less | **Yes.** Same % change as everywhere, and it makes the direction-of-tilt effect bigger or smaller |
:::

## Making Sense of the Orbital Factors Investigation {#esd-making-sense}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder + Analysis Question

| See: What did you observe? | Think | Wonder |
|---|---|---|
| How did the **direction** of Earth's tilt affect the amount of radiation reaching Earth's surface? | What do these observations make you think? | What questions do you have? |
| How did the **degree** of Earth's tilt affect the amount of radiation reaching Earth's surface? | | |
| How did the **eccentricity** of Earth's orbit affect the amount of radiation reaching Earth's surface? | | |

**Analysis Question:** Based on what you observed in the models, do you think Earth's changing orbit and tilt could be the **cause** of the patterns in total radiation reaching Earth at 65° N? Provide evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

Ideas your class should land on:

- Earth's **orbit** goes through a **~100,000-year cycle** between nearly circular and more oval. That changes how close Earth is to the Sun at different times of year.
- When Earth is **closer**, it receives **more** radiation; **farther**, it receives **less**. More radiation could make temperatures higher.
- Earth's **degree of tilt** goes through a **~41,000-year cycle between about 22.1° and 24.5°**. This changes the **angle** and **concentration** of sunlight at different latitudes, including 65° N.
- The **direction of tilt** goes through a **~26,000-year** wobble. At one extreme, the NH is tilted **toward** the Sun when Earth is closest; at the other, **away** from the Sun when closest. This also changes the angle and concentration of sunlight at 65° N.
- **Analysis:** Yes, these factors **could** cause the pattern. They change sunlight at 65° N on time scales of **tens of thousands to 100,000 years**, the same time scales as the insolation curve.
- **Wonder:** *How much does each factor matter? What was Earth's position in the past, and what is it now?*
:::

# Explain: Did Changes in Earth's Position Cause the Patterns of Radiation and Glacial-Interglacial Cycles? {#esd-explain}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧠 Using Models to Explain the Ice Ages

Now you'll **use your models with real orbital data** to test a claim: *changes in Earth's position (Milankovitch cycles) cause the changes in sunlight at 65° N and the glacial-interglacial cycles.*

A good **explanatory model**:

- **represents a system** (Sun, Earth, orbit, ice sheets)
- **shows or predicts relationships** between parts of the system
- uses **scientific vocabulary and labels**
- gives a **mechanism**: *how* one thing causes another
- is **based on real data**
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdOrbitPair = function(s) {
  const W = 300, H = 200, cy = 98, sunX = 138, L = 26, tr = s.tilt * Math.PI / 180;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", `Orbit model for ${s.when}: closest ${s.min} million km, farthest ${s.max} million km, tilt ${s.tilt} degrees, NH summer when ${s.toward ? "closer" : "farther"}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("display", "block");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1d33");
  svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", 150).attr("cy", cy).attr("rx", 122).attr("ry", 72).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7dd3fc").attr("stroke-width", 1.4);
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", sunX).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 22).attr("fill", "#f59e0b");
  const earths = [{x: 28, d: s.min, side: "L"}, {x: 272, d: s.max, side: "R"}];
  earths.forEach(e => {
    const summer = (s.toward && e.side === "L") || (!s.toward && e.side === "R");
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", e.side === "L" ? e.x + 13 : sunX + 22).attr("x2", e.side === "L" ? sunX - 22 : e.x - 13).attr("y1", cy).attr("y2", cy).attr("stroke", "#cbd5e1").attr("stroke-dasharray", "2,3");
    svg.append("text").attr("x", e.side === "L" ? 75 : 210).attr("y", cy - 8).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 10).text(`${e.d} M km`);
    if (summer) svg.append("circle").attr("cx", e.x).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 19).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#fde047").attr("stroke-width", 3);
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", e.x).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 12).attr("fill", "#bfdbfe").attr("stroke", "#1e3a8a");
    const sx = s.toward ? Math.sin(tr) : -Math.sin(tr);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", e.x - sx * L).attr("y1", cy + Math.cos(tr) * L).attr("x2", e.x + sx * L).attr("y2", cy - Math.cos(tr) * L).attr("stroke", "white").attr("stroke-width", 2.2);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", e.x + sx * (L + 6)).attr("y", cy - Math.cos(tr) * (L + 4)).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 10).attr("font-weight", "bold").text("N");
    svg.append("text").attr("x", e.x).attr("y", cy + 44).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", summer ? "#fde047" : "#93c5fd").attr("font-size", 10).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(summer ? "☀️ NH summer" : "NH winter");
  });
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 150).attr("y", 20).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 14).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(s.when);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 150).attr("y", H - 10).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").attr("font-size", 10).text(`Tilt ${s.tilt}° · NH summer when Earth is ${s.toward ? "closer" : "farther"}`);
  const rS = s.toward ? s.min : s.max;
  const Q = esdQ(rS, s.tilt);
  return {node: svg.node(), Q, rS};
}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Orbital Factors and Glacial Cycles Part 1

For **each shift** (144→130, 130→113, 25→9 kya):

1. On the model, **identify Earth's position during NH summer**. (For 25→9 kya, first **draw the tilt** and **label the distances** yourself.)
2. Complete the table for **Precession, Eccentricity and Tilt**: *Did it change? What will the effect be on (radiation reaching) 65° N in summer? Explain why* (think about the **amount** and **angle** of sunlight).
3. How will **summer in the NH** be impacted? Give evidence, and explain with words and/or a drawing.
4. How will the **ice sheets** in the NH be impacted? Give evidence.
5. Does your prediction **match** the July insolation at 65° N and the glacial-interglacial graph?

**Summarize:** Overall, how do these factors affect the **total** energy Earth receives, the **distribution** of sunlight, and over what **time scale**? How do they impact glacial-interglacial cycles?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your tables (try it first!)

**144 kya → 130 kya: toward an interglacial**

| Factor | Changed? | Effect on 65° N in summer | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Precession | No (NH toward Sun when closer at both times) | Still favors strong NH summers | NH summer stays on the close side of the orbit |
| Eccentricity | Yes: more oval (closest 145.6 → 143.8 M km) | More sunlight | NH summer is now even closer to the Sun, so more **amount** of sunlight |
| Tilt | Yes: 22.6° → 24.25° | More sunlight | Higher summer Sun, more direct **angle**, more concentrated beam |

→ Stronger NH summers → more snow and ice melt → **ice sheets shrink** → **interglacial**. ✅ Matches the graphs: insolation rises to a peak and temperature jumps to the warm 130 kya interglacial.

**130 kya → 113 kya: toward a glacial**

| Factor | Changed? | Effect on 65° N in summer | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Precession | Yes: flipped to NH away from Sun when closer | Less sunlight | NH summer now happens at the far side (155.6 M km) |
| Eccentricity | Barely (143.8/155.4 → 143.6/155.6 M km) | Almost none | Distances nearly the same |
| Tilt | Yes: 24.25° → 22.25° | Less sunlight | Lower summer Sun, beam more spread out |

→ Weaker NH summers → winter snow doesn't melt → **ice sheets grow** → **glacial**. ✅ Matches: insolation drops to a low at 113 kya and temperatures fall.

**25 kya → 9 kya: toward an interglacial**

| Factor | Changed? | Effect on 65° N in summer | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Precession | Yes (see the heads-up above): NH summer moved from the far side to the close side | More sunlight | NH summer happens closer to the Sun |
| Eccentricity | A little more oval (147.36/151.84 → 146.61/152.59 M km) | Slightly more | Makes the precession effect a bit stronger |
| Tilt | Yes: 22.3° → 24.25° | More sunlight | More direct summer Sun at 65° N |

→ Stronger NH summers → **ice sheets melt** → the end of the last ice age and our current **interglacial**. ✅ Matches: insolation peaks near 10 kya and temperature rises to today's level.

**Summarize (sample):** **Eccentricity** changes the **total** amount of energy Earth receives (a little) because it changes the distance to the Sun. The **degree** and **direction of tilt** change the **distribution** of sunlight, especially how much reaches high northern latitudes in summer. They act over **~23,000, ~41,000 and ~100,000 years**. When they combine to give **strong summers at 65° N**, ice sheets melt and Earth enters an **interglacial**; when summers are **weak**, snow builds up year after year and Earth enters a **glacial**.
:::

**Using a computational model to test your explanation.** Your packet uses an online model called *The Vostok Core and Milankovitch Cycles*. Below is an online version you can use anywhere.

### Top view and oblique view: today's orbit

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 340, H = 220, cx = 170, cy = 104;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", "Top view of Earth's orbit today: Earth is farthest from the Sun (aphelion) near the June solstice and closest (perihelion) near the December solstice")
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("max-width", "460px").style("display", "block").style("margin", "auto");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1d33");
  svg.append("ellipse").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("rx", 105).attr("ry", 62).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7dd3fc").attr("stroke-dasharray", "4,3");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx - 18).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 16).attr("fill", "#f59e0b");
  const E = (x, lab1, lab2, toward) => {
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 11).attr("fill", "#93c5fd");
    const t = 23.4 * Math.PI / 180, dir = toward;
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", x + dir * Math.sin(t) * 22).attr("y1", cy - Math.cos(t) * 22).attr("x2", x - dir * Math.sin(t) * 22).attr("y2", cy + Math.cos(t) * 22).attr("stroke", "white").attr("stroke-width", 2);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", x).attr("y", cy + 40).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", "bold").text(lab1);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", x).attr("y", cy + 54).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 10).text(lab2);
  };
  E(cx - 105, "Perihelion (closest)", "~Jan 3 · 147.1 M km", -1);
  E(cx + 105, "Aphelion (farthest)", "~Jul 4 · 152.1 M km", -1);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx - 105).attr("y", cy - 30).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#93c5fd").attr("font-size", 10).text("NH tilted away");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx + 105).attr("y", cy - 30).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fde68a").attr("font-size", 10).text("NH tilted toward");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 18).attr("fill", "white").attr("font-size", 12).attr("font-weight", "bold").text("Today's orbit (shape exaggerated)");
  return svg.node();
}
```

### The ice core and Milankovitch cycles

- The **Vostok ice core** came from a Russian-U.S. drilling project that finished drilling in 1998 at Vostok Station in **East Antarctica**. It reached **3,623 m** deep, and air bubbles trapped in the ice record the atmosphere's past.
- Serbian scientist **Milutin Milanković** worked out that orbital changes make the **seasonal and latitude-by-latitude** amount of sunlight change over time. These are called **Milankovitch cycles**.
- The model below uses the **EPICA Dome C** core (East Antarctica), which matches Vostok and extends the record to 800,000 years. Check boxes to add a **purple line** for each orbital factor. Each purple line is scaled so that **up = favors stronger NH summers**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof esdFactors = Inputs.checkbox(["Eccentricity", "Precession", "Tilt"], {label: "Add orbital factor(s):", value: []})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const maxT = 400;
  const tem = esdEdc.filter(d => d.t <= maxT);
  const orb = esdOrbit.filter(d => d.t <= maxT);
  const mT = d3.mean(tem, d => d.T), sT = d3.deviation(tem, d => d.T);
  const scaleTo = key => { const m = d3.mean(orb, d => d[key]), s = d3.deviation(orb, d => d[key]); return orb.map(d => ({t: d.t, v: mT + (d[key] - m) / s * sT * 0.8})); };
  const keys = {"Eccentricity": "e", "Precession": "closeness", "Tilt": "obl"};
  const all3 = esdFactors.length === 3;
  const lines = all3 ? [{name: "All 3 combined (July sunlight at 65° N)", pts: scaleTo("jul"), dash: null}]
    : esdFactors.map((f, i) => ({name: f, pts: scaleTo(keys[f]), dash: ["", "6,4", "2,3"][i]}));
  const marks = [
    Plot.rect(esdIG.filter(b => b.x1 <= maxT), {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -11, y2: 5, fill: "#facc15", fillOpacity: 0.25}),
    Plot.line(tem, {x: "t", y: "T", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    ...lines.map(l => Plot.line(l.pts, {x: "t", y: "v", stroke: "#9333ea", strokeWidth: 2.2, strokeDasharray: l.dash}))
  ];
  const legend = lines.length ? lines.map(l => `<span style="color:#9333ea;font-weight:700;">━ ${l.name}</span>`).join(" &nbsp; ") : "<i>Check a box to add an orbital factor.</i>";
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    title: "Antarctic temperature and orbital factors, last 400,000 years",
    width: Math.max(300, width), height: 300, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {domain: [maxT, 0], label: "Thousands of years ago"},
    y: {label: "Temperature vs. today (°C)", domain: [-11, 5], grid: true},
    marks: [...marks, Plot.tip(tem, Plot.pointerX({x: "t", y: "T", title: d => `${d.t} thousand years ago\nTemperature: ${d.T} °C\nJuly sunlight at 65° N: ${esdOrbit[d.t].jul} W/m²\nEccentricity ${esdOrbit[d.t].e} · Tilt ${esdOrbit[d.t].obl}°`}))]
  })}${(() => { const s = document.createElement("p"); s.style.cssText = "font-size:.9em;text-align:center;"; s.innerHTML = "⬛ Ice-core temperature &nbsp; " + legend; return s; })()}
  <p class="esd-caption">Purple lines are rescaled to fit the temperature axis; only their ups and downs matter. Data: EPICA Dome C (Jouzel et al. 2007) and Berger &amp; Loutre (1991), NOAA.</p></div>`;
}
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Orbital Factors and Glacial Cycles Part 2

- **Top view / Oblique view:** circle *closer to / farther from* for aphelion and perihelion, and *toward / away from* the Sun for the tilt at each. Then explain in your own words how Earth's tilt and orbit determine how much solar radiation **New York City** gets.
- **Practice:** temperature direction on the graph, how many cycles (2, 3, 4) in 400,000 years, and true/false: today is the warmest of the last 400,000 years.
- **Data Analysis 1–3:** Turn on **Eccentricity**, then **Precession**, then **Tilt**. True or false: each one **correlates** with (closely matches) temperature? Support with evidence.
- **4:** Which factor correlates **most**? **5:** Turn on **all 3**: is that line more or less closely related to temperature?
- **6–7:** Find a time when orbital factors and temperature **match closely**, and a time when they **don't**. State the time period and describe what you see.
- **Summarize:** evidence of correlation; have you established a **causal link** (how)?; what further questions do you have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Part 2 answers (try it first!)

- **Top/oblique view:** aphelion = **farther from**; perihelion = **closer to**. At aphelion (July) the NH tilts **toward** the Sun; at perihelion (January) it tilts **away**.
- **New York City:** NYC gets the most solar radiation in NH summer, when the NH tilts toward the Sun: the Sun is high and days are long. Distance matters much less; Earth is actually farthest from the Sun in July.
- **Practice:** **4** cycles; **False** (the interglacials about 125,000 and 330,000 years ago were warmer).
- **1. Eccentricity:** **True, partly.** Its ~100,000-year rhythm lines up with the timing of the big cycles (high around 125 and 330 kya). It doesn't match everywhere: around 400 kya eccentricity was very low but there was a long interglacial.
- **2. Precession:** **False** on its own. It rises and falls about every 23,000 years, including many times during glacials.
- **3. Tilt:** **Partly.** Its 41,000-year peaks line up with some warm-ups (about 130 and 335 kya) but there are extra peaks during cold times.
- **4.** **Eccentricity** best matches the overall ~100,000-year pacing.
- **5.** All 3 combined is **most closely** related: every big warm-up (terminations) starts during a strong peak in combined July sunlight.
- **6. Close match (example):** **135 → 128 kya**: combined sunlight rises to about 487 W/m² and temperature jumps about 10 °C into the warmest interglacial on the graph.
- **7. Poor match (example):** **About 218 kya** (highest sunlight peak, but only a small warm-up) or **about 173 kya** (a peak of 481 W/m² while temperatures stayed glacial).
- **Summarize:** There is a clear **correlation**. The models give a **mechanism** (stronger summers at 65° N → ice sheets melt), which supports a **causal link**, but the mismatches mean orbital factors are **not the only cause**. *What else amplifies the change?* (Next chapter: ice, oceans and CO₂.)
:::

## Summary Task {#esd-summary-task}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Summary Task

1. Explain how Earth's **orbital shape, degree of tilt, and direction of tilt** impact the **amount and distribution** of energy reaching Earth, and therefore affect **global ice sheets**.
2. How did using **models** give you evidence for **correlational and/or causal** relationships between orbital factors and glacial-interglacial cycles?
3. How did the **time scale** of each orbital factor compare to the time scale of glacial and interglacial cycles? What about all three combined?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)

1. **Orbital shape (eccentricity)** changes Earth's distance from the Sun, so it changes the **amount** of energy Earth receives. **Degree of tilt** and **direction of tilt** change the **distribution**: how directly sunlight hits high latitudes, and whether NH summer happens when Earth is closer or farther. When they combine to make **NH summers stronger**, more ice melts each summer than snow falls each winter, so **ice sheets shrink**. Weaker summers let **ice sheets grow**.
2. The flashlight model showed the **mechanism** (angle, spreading, distance). Using real orbital data in the models, we **predicted** stronger or weaker summers for each shift, and the predictions **matched** the insolation and temperature records. Matching predictions + a mechanism is evidence for **causation**, not just correlation.
3. Precession (**~23,000 years**) and tilt (**~41,000 years**) are faster than the **~100,000-year** glacial cycles. Eccentricity (**~100,000 years**) matches their length. All three combined produce the peaks of summer sunlight that line up with the start of each interglacial.
:::

::: {.key-idea}
**🌍 Class Consensus Model: Global Energy Budget**

- **Input:** solar radiation from the Sun
- **Eccentricity** affects the **amount** of solar energy input
- **Angle (degree) and direction of tilt** affect the **distribution** of that energy on Earth
- *Earth system = Earth + atmosphere.* You'll add **ice caps, oceans and greenhouse gases** to this model in the next chapters.

**Still to test:** Does the **output of the Sun itself** change, and could that explain glacial cycles?
:::

# Elaborate: How Well Does Activity from the Sun Correlate with Glacial-Interglacial Cycles? {#esd-elaborate}

::: {.elaborate-box}
## 🌞 Is the Sun Itself Changing?

**Guiding question:** *Did changes in the amount of radiation the Sun was emitting contribute to climate change events in the past?*

To claim a cause, you have to **rule out other possible causes**. So far, orbital factors change **where and when** sunlight arrives. But the Sun's own **output** could change too.
:::

## Solar Cycles {#esd-solar-cycles}

- **Sunspots** are dark, cooler patches on the Sun caused by strong magnetic fields. More sunspots go with a more **active** Sun that gives off slightly **more radiation**, especially ultraviolet (UV).
- Your packet's images show **more sunspots in 2002** and **fewer in 2010**. UV telescope images get **dimmer** over that time: less solar radiation.
- Scientists measure the Sun's output with **satellites** (since 1978) and reconstruct it further back using **sunspot records** (since the 1600s) and **isotope proxies** in tree rings and ice.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{ojs}
esdSunTempChart = function(startYear = 1880, highlight = false) {
  const tsi = esdTsi.filter(d => d.year >= startYear - 5);
  const gis = esdGis.filter(d => d.year >= startYear - 5);
  const tsiA = esdAvg11(tsi, "tsi").filter(d => d.year >= startYear);
  const gisA = esdAvg11(gis, "T").filter(d => d.year >= startYear);
  // map TSI (1360 to 1362.5 W/m²) onto the temperature axis (-0.6 to 1.4 °C)
  const toT = v => -0.6 + (v - 1360) * 0.8;
  const W = Math.max(300, width);
  const marks = [
    ...(highlight ? [Plot.rect([{x1: 1960, x2: 2025}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -0.6, y2: 1.4, fill: "#64748b", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
      Plot.text([{x: 1962, y: 1.3}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "Since 1960", textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11, fill: "currentColor"})] : []),
    ...(esdYearly ? [
      Plot.line(tsi.filter(d => d.year >= startYear), {x: "year", y: d => toT(d.tsi), stroke: "#ca8a04", strokeOpacity: 0.45, strokeWidth: 1}),
      Plot.line(gis.filter(d => d.year >= startYear), {x: "year", y: "T", stroke: "#dc2626", strokeOpacity: 0.4, strokeWidth: 1})] : []),
    Plot.line(tsiA, {x: "year", y: d => toT(d.v), stroke: "#ca8a04", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line(gisA, {x: "year", y: "v", stroke: "#dc2626", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.axisY({anchor: "left", label: "Temperature change (°C)", tickFormat: d => d.toFixed(1)}),
    Plot.axisY(d3.ticks(-0.6, 1.4, 5), {anchor: "right", label: "Solar irradiance (W/m²)", tickFormat: d => (1360 + (d + 0.6) / 0.8).toFixed(1), stroke: "#ca8a04", color: "#ca8a04"}),
    Plot.tip(gis.filter(d => d.year >= startYear), Plot.pointerX({x: "year", y: "T", title: d => { const s = esdTsi.find(x => x.year === d.year); return `${d.year}\nTemperature: ${d.T > 0 ? "+" : ""}${d.T} °C\nSolar irradiance: ${s ? s.tsi.toFixed(2) + " W/m²" : "n/a"}`; }}))
  ];
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    title: "Temperature vs. solar activity",
    subtitle: "Thick lines = 11-year averages. Red = global temperature, gold = Sun's output.",
    width: W, height: 320, marginLeft: 52, marginRight: 56, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: d => String(d), domain: [startYear, 2025]},
    y: {domain: [-0.6, 1.4], grid: true, axis: null},
    marks
  })}<p class="esd-caption">Temperature: NASA GISTEMP v4, compared to the 1951–1980 average. Solar irradiance: NOAA Climate Data Record (NRLTSI2), yearly averages.</p></div>`;
}
```

### The Solar Cycle

The **Solar Cycle** is the regular rise and fall in the number of **sunspots** and in solar radiation. **Solar minimum** = fewest sunspots and least radiation; **solar maximum** = the most.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
esdMinima = [1902, 1913.6, 1923.6, 1933.8, 1944.2, 1954.3, 1964.9, 1976.5, 1986.8, 1996.4, 2008.9, 2019.9]
```

```{ojs}
  cyc.push({n: 25, mid: 2024, len: null});

    ]

}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Solar Cycles (cycle questions 1–4)

1. Approximately how long are **solar cycles**?
2. Look back at the glacial-interglacial graph. Approximately how long are **those** cycles?
3. Do the **time scales** correlate?
4. Based on the lengths of these cycles, is there a **strong causal link** between changes in radiation from the Sun and glacial-interglacial cycling?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Solar Cycles answers (try it first!)

**Sunspots and temperature (1–4)**

1. Increasing radiation **increases the energy input** to Earth's system.
2. **Yes**, more radiation is more energy that can warm Earth, but the change over a solar cycle is small: about **1 W/m² out of 1,361 (less than 0.1%)**.
3. **Not always.** From about 1900 to 1955 both rose together. Since about 1960 solar output has been **flat or slightly decreasing** while temperature rose about **1 °C**.
4. Other factors can push temperature the other way: **air pollution (aerosols)**, **volcanic eruptions**, **ocean cycles**, and **greenhouse gases**.

**Cycle lengths (1–4)**

1. About **11 years**.
2. About **100,000 years** (before about 1 million years ago they came about every 41,000 years).
3. **No.** They differ by a factor of about 9,000.
4. **No strong causal link.** Solar cycles are far too short to build or melt ice sheets. Changes in Earth's **orbit** match the glacial time scale much better.

**Bottom line:** *Did the Sun's total output contribute to past climate change events?* It can cause small changes over decades to centuries, but **not** the glacial-interglacial cycles.
:::

# Evaluate: How Do We Know That Orbital Factors Are Not Causing Climate Change Today? {#esd-evaluate}

::: {.evaluate-box}
## 🕵️ Disproving Climate Skeptics

Some people claim today's warming is **natural**: just Earth's orbit or the Sun. Your task is to use **data** to test that claim. Look at what each factor is doing **now**, and compare it to what temperature is doing **now**.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const ev = {
    "Today's warming (1880 → 2021)": {a: 141, b: 0, color: "#dc2626", yrs: "about 140 years"},
    "End of the Younger Dryas (12,800 → 11,100 years ago)": {a: 12800, b: 11100, color: "#7c3aed", yrs: "about 1,700 years"},
    "Start of the last deglaciation (20,000 → 14,800 years ago)": {a: 20000, b: 14800, color: "#0b7285", yrs: "about 5,200 years"}
  }[esdEvent];
  const Tat = bp => { for (let i = 0; i < esdHolo.length - 1; i++) { const p = esdHolo[i], q = esdHolo[i + 1]; if (p.bp >= bp && bp >= q.bp) return p.T + (q.T - p.T) * (p.bp - bp) / (p.bp - q.bp); } return null; };
  const ta = Tat(ev.a);
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    title: "Last 22,000 years of global temperatures to present (2021)",
    subtitle: `${esdEvent.split(" (")[0]}: a 1.25 °C rise took ${ev.yrs}`,
    width: Math.max(300, width), height: 300, marginLeft: 48, marginRight: 14, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {domain: [22000, 0], label: "Years before present", tickFormat: d => d3.format(",")(d)},
    y: {domain: [-4, 2], label: "Global temperature (°C)", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rect([ev], {x1: "a", x2: "b", y1: -4, y2: 2, fill: ev.color, fillOpacity: 0.15}),
      Plot.ruleY([ta, ta + 1.25], {stroke: ev.color, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.line(esdHolo, {x: "bp", y: "T", stroke: "#2563eb", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([esdHolo[esdHolo.length - 1]], {x: "bp", y: "T", fill: "#dc2626", r: 5}),
      Plot.tip(esdHolo, Plot.pointerX({x: "bp", y: "T", title: d => `${d3.format(",")(d.bp)} years ago\n${d.T > 0 ? "+" : ""}${d.T} °C`}))
    ]
  })}<p class="esd-caption">Values read by eye from the packet's NASA graph (climate.nasa.gov; Shakun et al. 2012 and Marcott et al. 2013 reconstructions plus NASA measurements), so they are approximate. On this scale, the last 140 years look like a vertical line at the right edge.</p></div>`;
}
```

## 🔑 Check your Performance Task Data answers (try it first!)

**Historical Global Temperature** (read from the graph, so approximate)

1. Today's event: about **140 years** (1880s → 2021).
2. Next fastest: the end of the **Younger Dryas cold snap**, about **12,800 → 11,100 years ago**: about **1,700 years** (roughly 12× slower than today).
3. From 20,000 years ago: about **5,200 years** (to about 14,800 years ago).

**9 kya → today**

1–2. At **9 kya**, the NH was tilted **toward** the Sun when Earth was **closer** (146.61 M km), tilt **24.25°**: NH summer at the **close** side. **Today**, NH summer happens at the **far** side (152.14 M km), tilt **23.4°**.
3. NH summers should be **weaker** (less sunlight at 65° N): precession flipped and tilt decreased. Eccentricity changed a little (slightly less oval).
4. Toward a **glacial** period: very slow cooling over thousands of years.

**Solar output:** Since about **1960**, the Sun's 11-year average output has been **flat or slightly decreasing**, while global temperature rose about **1 °C**.
:::

## ✅ Earth-Sun Dynamics Rubric Checklist

Use this checklist (from the **Earth-Sun Dynamics Rubric**) before you turn in your explanation.

**Explanation:** use **multiple lines of valid and reliable evidence** to explain why scientists are sure **natural cycles are not causing climate change today**, including:

- What has been happening with **each factor** (eccentricity, tilt, direction of tilt, solar output) **in recent history up until now**, and what will happen in the **near future**
- The **overall impact** these factors are having on the **total amount** and **distribution** of energy on Earth
- How these factors relate to **current temperature changes** on Earth
- **Evidence linked to your explanation** with scientific logic and reasoning

**Cause and Effect:** clearly state whether there is a **correlation and/or a causal link** between orbital factors and glacial/interglacial periods, and whether they explain the **present**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Sample explanation (try writing yours first!)

**Claim:** Orbital factors and solar cycles are **not** causing today's warming or the melting of ice caps.

**Evidence and reasoning:**

- **Orbit:** Since 9,000 years ago, the direction of tilt flipped (NH summer now happens at the far point, 152.14 M km) and tilt decreased (24.25° → 23.4°, still decreasing). July sunlight at 65° N fell from about 469 to 427 W/m². Our models show weaker NH summers should let ice **grow**, a slow move toward a **glacial** period. That matches the slow cooling over thousands of years before the 1800s. In the near future these factors keep changing only very slowly (tilt keeps decreasing for about 10,000 years). They can't cause warming at all, let alone fast warming.
- **Sun:** The Sun's output rises and falls every ~11 years by less than 0.1%, and since about 1960 its average has been flat or slightly lower. Temperature rose about 1 °C over the same time, so they are **not correlated** now.
- **Rate:** Natural 1.25 °C rises took about 1,700 to 5,200 years. Today's took about 140 years. Orbital changes act over **tens of thousands of years**.
- **Cause and effect:** Orbital factors are **correlated** with glacial-interglacial cycles, and our models give a **mechanism**, so they are a likely **cause** of past ice ages. But today they point toward cooling, so they **cannot be the cause** of current warming. Something else must be adding energy to Earth's system.
:::

|---|---|

| Stronger NH summers → ice sheets melt; weaker → ice sheets grow (144→130, 130→113, 25→9 kya) | Explain Part 1 |
| Since 9 kya, orbital changes have weakened NH summers: slow cooling expected | Evaluate: 9 kya → today |
| Solar cycles last ~11 years; solar output flat/slightly down since ~1960 | Elaborate; Evaluate |
| Today's 1.25 °C rise took ~140 years vs. 1,700+ years for natural warming | Evaluate: Historical Global Temperature |

**Still to figure out:** If it isn't the orbit or the Sun, **what is adding energy to Earth's system now?** Many people think **greenhouse gases** and **human activities**. That's the next chapter: [Climate Feedbacks](unit4-climate-feedbacks.qmd).

# Chapter Summary

| Key Concept | Details |
|---|---|
| **65° N summer sunlight** | Controls whether winter snow survives; rises and falls between about 390 and 500 W/m² (July) |
| **Glacial-interglacial cycles** | Ice ages with short warm interglacials about every 100,000 years for the last ~800,000 years |
| **Direction of tilt (precession)** | Axis wobble ~26,000 yr; NH summer lines up with closest approach about every 19,000–24,000 yr. Changes distribution |
| **Degree of tilt (obliquity)** | 22.1° ↔ 24.5° every ~41,000 yr; now 23.44° and decreasing. Changes distribution |
| **Shape of orbit (eccentricity)** | ~0.0034 to ~0.058, cycles of ~100,000 and ~405,000 yr; now 0.0167. Changes total amount (a little) and strengthens precession |
| **Mechanism** | Strong NH summers → ice sheets melt → interglacial; weak summers → ice sheets grow → glacial |
| **Correlation vs. causation** | Orbital factors correlate with ice ages and have a mechanism, but don't match perfectly; feedbacks matter too |
| **Solar cycle** | ~11 years, under 0.1% change in output; far too short to drive ice ages |
| **Today** | Orbit → weaker NH summers (slow cooling); Sun flat/slightly down since ~1960; temperature up ~1.2 °C since 1880 → not natural cycles |

```{=html}
<script>
(function() {
  var cards = [
    {
      text: "Earth has summer when it is closest to the Sun.",
      type: "Myth",

    },
    {

    },

      type: "Myth",

    },
    {

      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "That's correlation, not causation. To claim a cause you need a mechanism (like the flashlight model) and you need to rule out other causes. That's why we tested both the orbit and the Sun."
    },
    {
      text: "Today's warming is happening much faster than the natural warming at the end of the last ice age.",
      type: "Fact",

    }

    var fb = el('esdmf-feedback');
    fb.style.display = 'block';
    fb.style.background = correct ? 'rgba(0,184,148,0.22)' : 'rgba(214,48,49,0.22)';
    fb.style.border = '1px solid ' + (correct ? '#00b894' : '#e17055');
    fb.innerHTML = '<strong>' + (correct ? '✅ Correct! ' : '❌ That\'s a ' + card.type + '! ') + '</strong>' + card.explanation;
    el('esdmf-myth').disabled = true;
    el('esdmf-fact').disabled = true;
    el('esdmf-myth').style.opacity = (choice === 'Myth') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('esdmf-fact').style.opacity = (choice === 'Fact') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('esdmf-next').style.display = 'block';
  };
  window.esdmfNext = function() { idx++; updateCard(); };
  window.esdmfRestart = function() {
    idx = 0; score = 0; answered = 0;
    el('esdmf-card').style.display = 'flex';
    el('esdmf-myth').style.display = 'block';
    el('esdmf-fact').style.display = 'block';
    el('esdmf-done').style.display = 'none';
    el('esdmf-score').textContent = '0';
    el('esdmf-total').textContent = '0';
    updateCard();
  };
  updateCard();
})();
</script>
```

# End-of-Chapter Quiz {#end-of-chapter-quiz}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function esdFinalQuiz(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="font-family:'Inter',sans-serif; max-width:720px; margin:18px auto;"></div>`;
  const header = html`<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0b7285 0%,#0a3d62 100%);color:#fff;border-radius:14px 14px 0 0;padding:18px 24px;">
    <div style="font-size:1.1em;font-weight:700;">📝 ${title}</div>
    <div style="font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.85;margin-top:4px;">Select an answer for each question.</div>
  </div>`;
  const body = html`<div style="border:1.5px solid #9bd3dd;border-top:none;border-radius:0 0 14px 14px;overflow:hidden;background:#f0fbfd;padding:16px;"></div>`;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.className = "esd-fq-opt";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        const all = card.querySelectorAll("button.esd-fq-opt");
        all.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; b.style.background = "#f8fafc"; b.style.color = "#475569"; });
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";btn.style.color="#276749";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";btn.style.color="#9b2c2c";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          const c = all[qq.correct];
          c.style.borderColor="#48bb78";c.style.background="#f0fff4";c.style.color="#276749";c.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";fb.style.borderRadius="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    fb.className = "esd-fb";
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```
